title: Non-Hermitian Statistical Geometry
authors: Xi Hu, Yan-Qiong Ma, Su-Peng Kou
abstract: Particle exchange in two dimensions gives rise to quantum statistics beyond the boson-fermion dichotomy, with central roles in fractional quantum Hall physics, topological quantum computation, and strongly correlated quantum matter. In conventional topological phases, microscopic exchange geometry is compressed into rigid braid and fusion data. We develop a theory of non-Hermitian statistical geometry in which relaxing Hermiticity softens these exchange data into a larger complex space of spectral and relative-geometric degrees of freedom. For two adjacent braid generators, a single projective exchange spectrum is insufficient: their relative eigenline geometry supplies an additional gauge-invariant modulus. On the generic irreducible two-channel branch, braid consistency locks these coordinates through an exact spectrum-geometry relation. Using Riesz projectors and Kato transport, we realize this geometry in a five-arm Kitaev-Majorana network and test spectral and relative-geometric responses in an independent two-dimensional four-vortex Kitaev model. Finite-time dynamics tests the exchange operation, microscopic fusion sewing tests its composition across fusion descriptions, and matched-spectrum controls isolate the role of relative geometry. Nonzero projective Kato curvature shows that braid-consistent, fusion-coherent exchange can depend on the control path. Non-Hermiticity thus exposes exchange geometry, braid consistency re-locks it, fusion coherence further constrains it, and projective flatness determines when geometric exchange becomes intrinsically topological.
summary: This work introduces non-Hermitian statistical geometry to study quantum statistics beyond the standard boson-fermion dichotomy. It develops a theory showing that relaxing Hermiticity enriches the exchange dynamics, which are then constrained by consistency conditions derived from braid and fusion algebra. The results provide a deep link between complex spectral data and geometric properties in topological matter.
main_problem: The paper develops a theory of non-Hermitian statistical geometry to understand how quantum statistics behave when the underlying microscopic Hamiltonian is non-Hermitian, relaxing the rigidity found in conventional topological phases.
main_result: Non-Hermiticity enriches the exchange response by allowing relative channel amplification alongside relative phase, leading to a sequence where braid consistency, fusion coherence, and projective flatness sequentially constrain the exchange geometry.
method: The authors use non-Hermitian generalizations of topological concepts, employing Kato transport, analyzing relative eigenline geometry, and testing consistency via generalized braiding and fusion equations.
model_or_system: The theory applies to particle exchange in two dimensions, relevant to fractional quantum Hall physics and strongly correlated quantum matter. It analyzes the extension of conventional anyon theory into non-Hermitian regimes, using models like the Kitaev-Majorana network.
key_observables: Projective exchange spectrum ($q$), relative eigenline geometry ($x$), projective Kato curvature, and various coherence residuals ($\epsilon_{	ext{micro pent}}$, $\eta_{	ext{hex}}$).
important_parameters: The non-Hermiticity parameter (relaxing Hermiticity), the level $k$ of $SU(2)_k$, and the coupling strength $J_{	ext{split}}$ in finite-chain calculations.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on extending rigid unitary exchange data into a complex space and assumes the applicability of concepts like the Artin relation and the Pentagon/Hexagon equations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the relationship between the single-exchange spectrum and relative geometry via the Artin relation, and later show convergence diagnostics for small-loop holonomy tests confirming predicted analytic curvature values.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first introducing the non-Hermitian framework, establishing the exact spectrum-geometry locking relation ($x = q + q^{-1} - 1$), and then rigorously testing this geometry using complex fusion and loop coherence diagnostics in finite-chain models.
why_interesting: The framework provides a powerful mathematical tool to study how topological constraints break down or evolve when physical symmetries (like Hermiticity) are broken, which is highly relevant for understanding dissipative or open quantum systems in condensed matter.
